summary: Describes how to set up secure media connections over TLS using the Session Description Protocol. It defines the TCP/TLS protocol identifier and a fingerprint attribute that names the certificate the other side will present. It clarifies how multiple fingerprints are used. It replaces RFC 4572.

eli5.summary: Two people agree on a secret meeting place by letter. This adds a line to the letter saying what the other person's ID card will look like, so you can spot an impostor.

subtitle: How a media stream described in SDP can run over TLS, with a certificate fingerprint standing in for a trusted signer.

tldr.problem: Two endpoints that set up a media stream through SDP often want it encrypted and authenticated, but they usually cannot get certificates signed by a well-known certification authority.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8122 defines the SDP protocol identifier TCP/TLS and a fingerprint attribute that carries a secure hash of the certificate the endpoint will present, so a self-signed certificate can be checked against the session description.
tldr.outcome: It works only as far as the SDP itself is protected. RFC 8122 replaces RFC 4572 and is updated by RFC 8844.

today: RFC 8122 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4572 and is updated by RFC 8844.

sections.title: Why SDP Needs TLS and Fingerprints
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) describes multimedia sessions. RFC 4145 lets a session description set up a connection-oriented media stream, but the only transport it directly supports is TCP. RFC 8122 extends that to the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol, so a stream can have confidentiality, data integrity and authentication.

TLS leaves open how a protocol on top of it should interpret and validate authentication certificates. RFC 8122 answers that for connection-oriented media. The difficulty is that the endpoints usually cannot get a certificate signed by a well-known certification authority (CA). CAs often charge, the administrative overhead is substantial, and addresses and host names may be dynamic, for example handed out by DHCP.

The answer is a certificate fingerprint: a secure hash of the certificate placed in the session description. If the certificate offered in the TLS handshake matches the fingerprint, the endpoints can trust even a self-signed certificate, provided the integrity of the SDP description is assured.
sections.eli5: Buying an official ID card is expensive and slow. So instead, you write down a short code that matches your home-made ID card, and the other person checks the card against the code.

sections.title: Operating Modes and the Threat Model
sections.content:
SDP sessions work in two modes. In advertised mode a server publishes a description (for example over the Session Announcement Protocol) and recipients connect to the addresses in it. In offer-answer mode two participants negotiate: one offers a session from its own perspective and the other answers. This is the mode used by the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP).

The RFC walks through three kinds of attacker. A passive listener threatens only confidentiality, and almost any mode of TLS covers that. An attacker who can send traffic but not modify valid traffic matters in offer-answer mode, where it could impersonate an endpoint or sit in the middle; TLS endpoint certificates thwart this. The most serious attacker can modify or redirect the session descriptions, such as a compromised SIP proxy server. Neither TLS nor anything built on it can protect against that, so the SDP itself must be secured, for example with S/MIME in SIP.

If two endpoints have no prior relationship, a self-signed certificate cannot generally be trusted. But if the SDP integrity is assured, the description itself can be treated as the prior relationship, and the fingerprint inside it vouches for the certificate.
sections.eli5: A sneaky listener can only overhear. A pushy stranger might pretend to be your friend, so you check ID. But if someone is swapping the letters themselves, no ID check helps, so the letters need their own lock.

sections.title: The TCP/TLS Identifier and the Fingerprint Attribute
sections.content:
The m line of an SDP description names the transport protocol. RFC 8122 defines the identifier TCP/TLS, meaning TLS over TCP. It names only the transport, so an m line using it MUST also carry a format identifier that says which application runs over TLS. Such sessions follow the procedures of RFC 4145 and use its setup and connection attributes.

Endpoints MUST provide a certificate fingerprint. It is a secure one-way hash of the DER form of the X.509 certificate. In SDP it is an a line holding the name of the hash function, then the hash as uppercase hexadecimal bytes separated by colons, the same style used by openssl and browser certificate managers. The attribute can be session-level, applying to every TLS session with no media-level fingerprint, or media-level.

The defined hash function names are SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, MD5 and MD2, with SHA-256 preferred. Implementations MUST NOT use MD2 or MD5 to calculate fingerprints or to verify fingerprints calculated with them. They are listed only so implementations can recognize them.
sections.eli5: The fingerprint line is a short code for your ID card, written in a fixed style: the name of the code-making machine, then the code in pairs of letters and digits. Everyone must use the same style so it can be compared.

sections.title: Multiple Fingerprints and Matching
sections.content:
An m line can have several fingerprint attributes. They may be the same certificate hashed with different functions, or fingerprints for several certificates, for instance when separate certificates are used for RTP and RTCP, or when it is not known which certificate will be used.

An endpoint MUST, as a minimum, calculate a fingerprint with SHA-256 and with the hash function used for the signature on the certificate, for each possible certificate. Including the signature hash keeps it interoperable with strict implementations of RFC 4572. Either can be omitted if the endpoint includes a stronger hash that it knows the peer supports, if the peer is known not to support the hash, or if local policy mandates stronger algorithms. With multiple certificates, the same set of hash functions MUST be used for each.

The receiving endpoint MUST select the set of fingerprints that use its most preferred hash function among those offered, and verify that each certificate used matches one fingerprint in that set. If a certificate matches none, the endpoint MUST NOT establish the TLS connection. The attribute does not name a specific certificate, so the endpoint compares against certificate hashes to find a match.
sections.eli5: You may write several codes for the same ID card, made with different machines. The other person picks the machine they like best and checks that the card matches. If it matches nothing, the door stays shut.

sections.title: Certificates and Endpoint Identity
sections.content:
If the SDP travels over something that gives integrity protection, such as HTTP over TLS or S/MIME, the certificate securing the media connection MAY assert any syntactically valid identity. Hop-by-hop protection such as the SIPS scheme is also considered sufficient for this mode, though the security section points out the cost.

If the SDP is not integrity-protected, the certificate MUST certify an appropriate identity: either the connection address in the c line (an iPAddress or dNSName subjectAltName matching exactly, with no wildcard patterns), or, where the SDP was carried by a protocol such as SIP that identifies participants by URI, a uniformResourceIdentifier subjectAltName matching the identity of the endpoint that generated the SDP. Matching follows RFC 5280, and endpoints SHOULD consistently provide the same certificate for each identity.

The endpoint acting as TLS server (the setup:passive role) MUST always present a certificate. If it does not match the fingerprint, the client MUST end the connection with a bad_certificate error. With offer-answer, the client (setup:active) MUST also present one and the server MUST request it; a missing or non-matching client certificate also ends the connection with bad_certificate.

A connection can outrace the answer. An offerer using setup:passive or setup:actpass MUST start listening as soon as it sends the offer, but MUST NOT assume the data is valid until it has seen a matching fingerprint in the answer. Without offer-answer (for example SDP sent over the Session Announcement Protocol) there is no secure channel for client fingerprints, so servers MAY request client certificates, which SHOULD be signed by a well-known CA, or allow clients to connect without one.
sections.eli5: The grown-up who opens the door always shows ID. If the ID does not match the code in the letter, the door slams shut. Sometimes the visitor has to show ID too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Offering TCP/TLS does not oblige an endpoint to accept any TLS connection with the right fingerprint; it still has to run normal TLS negotiation and check that the cipher and MAC meet the application's needs. An offered TLS_NULL_WITH_NULL_NULL cipher SHOULD be rejected in almost every scenario.

The protocol that carries the SDP (SIP, MGCP and so on) is responsible for its integrity, and SHOULD use its own security or a lower-layer service such as TLS or IPsec, with strong message authentication and replay protection. When that is not possible, end systems SHOULD keep a cache of certificates previously presented, tell users about an unsecured certificate from a new party and strongly warn if a known party presents a different one. That makes the mechanism equivalent to SSH: vulnerable at first contact, able to detect later attacks. Users SHOULD NOT be notified about certificates in SDP sent over an integrity-protected channel.

Hop-by-hop protection such as SIPS was accepted because it was the integrity mechanism most likely to be deployed in the short to medium term, but SDP integrity is then open to attack by compromised or malicious middleboxes such as SIP proxies. The RFC also says that RTP and RTCP over a connection-oriented channel are out of scope (see RFC 7850) and that TLS is not always the right choice.

Compared with RFC 4572, the preferred hash moves from SHA-1 to SHA-256, MD2 and MD5 are deprecated, and clearer multiple-fingerprint handling allows hash agility and incremental deployment of stronger hashes.
sections.eli5: The ID check is only as safe as the letter carrying it. If a stranger can rewrite the letter, the check is useless, so keep a notebook of faces you have met and get suspicious when one changes.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA updated the registrations from RFC 4572 to point to this document. The TCP/TLS value is registered in the SDP proto registry and fingerprint in the att-field registry, usable at session and media level. New formats for TCP/TLS SHOULD have an associated MIME registration. The "Hash Function Textual Names" registry now refers to RFC 8122, and new hash functions MUST be defined by Standards Track RFCs that update or obsolete RFC 3279.
sections.eli5: The official list of names was updated so everyone looks up the same words for this feature.
